The preheating analysis results, in turn, are still in an early stage and require further research to provide an accurate quantification of the effect of this process on residual stress and distortion in the tank floor. Resolving failures in molten salt TES tanks is crucial not only for CSP but also for other applications considering these technologies. Despite the deficiencies of early implementations, molten salt TES remains one of the most mature, scalable, and cost-effective TES technologies. Addressing current failures by perfecting tank design and fabrication is fundamental to unlocking its full potential beyond CSP, extending its application to nuclear, superhot geothermal, and industrial process heat. v This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Introduction 1.1 Background Current solar tower CSP plants use a two-tank system with molten salt for heat storage (TES). The hot salt tanks are usually built with stainless steel (SS) 347H, following design and material recommendations from the American Petroleum Institute’s (API) 650 [1] and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers’ (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC), Section II [2]. Multiple failures in molten salt hot tanks in solar tower CSP plants [3], including Crescent Dunes in the United States, Gemasolar in Spain, Noor III in Morocco, and Cerro Dominador in Chile, have resulted in major financial losses and reduced trust in the technology. During the first phase of the project funded by the Department of Energy (DOE) – Solar Energy Technologies Office (SETO), agreement 38475—'Failure analysis of molten salt tanks for in-service CSP plants'—the primary causes for these failures were analyzed.
